speechtext:
Hon. MACKENZIE KING (Minister of Labour) moved for leave to introduce Bill

(No. 101) to provide for the investigating of combines, monopolies,	trusts and
mergers which may enhance prices or restrict competition to the detriment of consumers.
Carried.
Did the hon. gentleman give any explanation?

The somewhat lengthy title of this Bill may help to explain its scope and purpose. The short title is the Combines Investigation Act.	As human
ingenuity has devised a great many forms of combination for the purpose of effecting an increase in prices, or the restriction of competition, an effort has been made in this measure to give a definition of the word 'combine' sufficiently comprehensive to embrace all forms of combination which may have this effect, and in particular to make it clear that this measure shall have reference to all such forms of combination as are popularly known as monopolies, trusts, mergers and combines. The legislation differs in some particulars from legislation of a like nature which has been introduced in other countries in that it is not aimed against combines or mergers as such, but rather against the exercise on the part of combines, mergers or monopolies, in an unfair manner, of the powers which they may get from that form of organization. This is an age of organization and not merely of local or national competition but of world-wide competition and any industry or any nation which wishes to hold its own in the field of com-petitipn must do much in the way of perfecting organization. A highly organized industry should, from the facilities it has of improving production, lead to greater efficiency and economies of one kind and another, which should, on the whole, benefit the consuming public. But, we know that in other countries, and possibly also in this country, organizations have not always used their corporate powers to the . advantage of the consumers, but have taken, in some cases, possibly, an unfair advantage to themselves. This measure seeks to afford the means of conserving to the public some of the benefits which arise from large organizations of capital for the purpose of business and commerce. It is organized society which alone makes the organization of capital and industry possible, and the people have a right to expect, and to look to the government to see that their rights shall be conserved and that their liberties shall not be curtailed by, privileges which they permit others to enjoy.
Who is to initiate the investigation?

Perhaps it would be well if I were to explain somewhat in detail the procedure suggested by this measure. It is provided that the Act shall be under the Minister of Labour and that in connection with the administration of the Act a registrar of boards of investigation shall be appointed.
In	all measures	of this	kind	thataffect private interests and at the same time public rights there are two factors which have to be kept constantly in mind. There is first of all the desirability of securing	the	minimum of	interference with private business where that	business	is	conducted	in	a	fairand	proper	way,	and on	the	other
hand the desirability of providing a ready and efficient means for individuals or the public to secure their due rights where these rights are interfered with or encroached upon by any corporation. These two objects, have, it is hoped, been kept in mind in the drafting of this measure. It is believed that the Bill as introduced will afford a ready and convenient means whereby parties who have reason to believe that any combination is unduly enhancing prices or unfairly restricting competition, may obtain an investigation, and an effective remedy against evils which may be found to exist. This, it is sought to obtain in the first place by providing that six or more persons who feel that a combine exists and that prices have been enhanced or competition restricted by reason of such combine to the detriment of the consumer, may make application to a judge of the high court for an order to grant an investigation. The judge may, if he so desires, call before him witnesses, but all that is necessary is for the judge to assure himself before granting such order that a prime facie case has been made out. The judge, if satisfied there is reasonable ground for believing that a combine exists which is injurious to trade or which is operating to the detriment of consumers, and that it is in the public interest an investigation should be held, may direct or rather shall direct $n investigation under the provisions of this Act.
When the judge issues an order for an investigation the order is to be directed to the minister who is thereupon to call each of the parties concerned to name a member on the board of investigation. The Act in this particular proceeds along lines somewhat similar to the procedure under the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act. The parties who have made the complaint are called upon to name a representative on this board of investigation, the parties concerned in the alleged combine are called upon to name a representative on their behalf, and the two gentlemen thus chosen are given opportunity of centering together with a view of selecting a third person (who



must in this particular case be a judge) to act as chairman of the board of investigation. Failing agreement the minister appoints the chairman. The board thus constituted shall have all the powers of a court of record; it shall have power of summoning witnesses, of ordering the production of documents, of taking evidence under oath. When the board has duly investigated the matters before it, it is the duty of the board to draw up a report and submit that report to the minister who is obliged to give it publicity by publishing it in the ' Canada Gazette/ by sending copies to the parties concerned, by distributing copies to the press if so desired, and by supplying copies to any other parties who may make application. Perhaps it would be well to read the section which refers to the board of investigation:
The board shall expeditiously and fully and carefully inquire into the matters referred to it and all matters affecting the merits thereof, including the question of whether or not the price or rental of any article concerned has been unreasonably enhanced or competition in the supply thereof unduly restricted in consequence of a combine, and shall make a full and detailed report thereon to the minister, which report shall set forth the various proceedings and steps taken by the board for the purpose of fully and carefully ascertaining all the facts and circumstances connected with the alleged combine, including such findings and reeom-mendations as in the opinion of the hoard are in accordance with the merits and requirements of the case.
There are certain classes of evils in the remedying of which it is believed publicity is more effective than penalty. It may not be that publicity will in all cases prove an effective remedy, but certainly in industrial matters it has many times in the past proven to be effective. While this Act provides machinery of a nature calculated to let in the light on the workings of these , large corporations when it is believed they are operating in a manner unfair to the consumer, and while it is believed that much good will be accomplished in this way, the legislation does not rely entirely upon publicity to bring about the desired remedy. There are other remedies proposed, and one is the remedy already existing in connection under other legislation with respect in certain cases to such articles as are protected by the tariff. The statute in this particular gives authority to the Governor in Council where the board reports that prices have been unduly enhanced or that competition is being unfairly restricted in virtue of the protection given to a particular article to reduce the tariff on that particular article or to remove the duty altogether.
Then, there is another class of combination which it is hoped this measure may be the means of preventing. I refer to the Mr. KING.
case of persons holding patents and who exercise their exclusive rights and privileges to restrict competition. In section 22 of the Act there is this provision:
In case the owner or holder of any patent issued under the Patent Act has made use of the exclusive rights and privileges which, as such owner or holder he controls, so as unduly to limit the facilities for transporting, producing, manufacturing, supplying, storing or dealing in any article which may be a subject of trade or commerce or so as un- -duly to restrain or injure trade or commerce in relation to any such article or unduly to prevent, limit or lessen the manufacture or production of any article or unreasonably to enhance the price thereof, or purchase, barter, sale, transportation, storage or supply of any article such patent shall be liable to be revoked.
The clause then sets forth the steps that may be taken for the revoking of the patent where an adverse report has been made by a board in such a case.
Then there is a further clause which provides that where a board finds any combination has been guilty of enhancing prices or unfairly restricting competition to the detriment of the consumers, if the guilty parties persist in the conduct which has been reported against, they shall be guilty of an indictable offence and liable to a penalty not exceeding $1,000 and costs for each day that they continue to offend after the expiration of ten days from the date of publication of the report of the board in the 'Canada Gazette/
These are the main features of the measure, Mr. Speaker. A good part of the Bill is taken up with the setting out the machinery for investigation, a part of it relates to the meetings of the board, the remuneration and expenses of the board and the taking of evidence, and there are a few miscellaneous clauses. I think, however, what I have said will be sufficient as an outline of the Bill.	[DOT]
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

I would ask the government if the rumour is true that a deputation from Montreal waited on the government yesterday to ask that they be granted the privilege of placing a dam across the St. Lawrence river. If so, has any decision been arrived at?
There was a deputation consisting of representatives of the company which proposes to develop the power, and that deputation presented certain statements to the Committee of the Privy Council.
Was any decision arrived at?

No, it was understood that they would present the modified plans to the International Waterways Commission, and that commission would give an opportunity to the navigation interests and those who might naturally be opposed to any obstructions to navigation, to be heard. After that the 'matter would come again before the government for consideration.
Has a day for hearing that deputation been arranged for?
No, the commission will arrange that.

Referring to the request preferred yesterday that the report of a certain fishery commission should be laid on the table, so far as I understand the case, it is this. Three commissioners were originally appointed. One of them was afterwards elevated to the bench and consequently ceased to act as a commissioner. Another was appointed in his place, and these three commissioners, duly constituted, made their report. The cause of the delay, as I understand it, is that the commissioner, who was elevated to the bench, has not signed the report. I do not see that he has any jurisdiction to sign, and therefore the reason given by the Prime Minister yesterday is not a good one for withholding the report.

PATERSON (Minister of Customs), _ The House has been favoured with a very gratifying budget 66i
statement this session, much the same as statements presented in sessions gone by. I think it has given universal satisfaction to the House and country to have heard and read the truthful recital of the favoured conditions of trade and commerce and the prosperity throughout this country. There is no difference of opinion regarding the fact that we are in this respect a highly favoured people, but there is this distinction between the members on the two sides . of the House. Our opponents claim that this prosperity in which we all rejoice, is not due in any measure at all to any action or policy of this government. As t-he hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) has said, our Finance Minister is not to toe credited with any portion of the benefits we are enjoying, as none of these benefits is due to his management of our financal affairs, but is due solely to the good harvests and the industry of our people. No one will doubt that we have had good harvests; no one will doubt .that we had a good harvest last year and that we have an industrial people. But what puzzles one is this. If these are to be accepted as the sole reason for our prosperity, and if the government have had nothing whatever to do with bringing about the condition of things which prevails, did we not have good harvests when our Conservative friends were in power? Did we not have fruitful fields then as now? Did we not have an industrial people then as now? Therefore, if the prosperity now abounding in Canada is due to these causes alone, how is it that we had such a period of depression, when precisely the same causes were at work under the old Conservative administration? That there was stagnation and depression and anything but a feeling of buoyancy when our friends opposite were in power, every one knows. That there is a buoyant feeling now and abundant prosperity every one likewise knows. How then do you account for the depression which then existed? How do you account for the prosperity which now prevails? The difference can only be due to the fact that the Liberal party know better how to utilize the benefits which a kind Providence has given us than did our opponents. I know of no other reason. If there be any other, will hon. gentlemen opposite give it?
Did the same conditions .prevail?
The same conditions prevailed-good harvests and an industrial people.	.
Did the same conditions prevail from 1874 to 1878?

We had abundant harvests and an industrial people and yet

under the Conservative regime we had depression. We had not then the buoyancy we have now or the prosperity. Hon. gentlemen opposite laugh. I do not object to their having a little pleasure, but I would like to have a little myself. I do not just see where the joke comes in, but they are able to see jokes sometimes where no one else can.
The joke "is right ahead of you.

And the principal joker seems to have got frightened and gone out -not an unusual sight in this House. Hon. gentlemen opposite make statements, broad statements, which they cannot verify, and which ought not to be made by responsible men. What are they? You have heard the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden), on more than one occasion, say that the Liberal party had violated every plank in the platform which they adopted in 1893.
Hear, hear.

Hear, hear, an hon. gentleman says. He is of the same belief yet, every one of them? If hon. gentlemen rejoice in their ignorance of the facts of the case I cannot help it, but I propose to read to the House the planks of the platform of the Liberal party adopted in 1893 and in the light of what has transpired I am going to ask this House and the people of this country if the men who dare to say that we have violated and broken every plank in that platform are not men who have told what is not true. Thus, after this, if any man endorses the statement that we have carried out none of the planks that we laid down, he sins with a full knowledge of the facts. Ten resolutions were adopted at that grand Liberal convention, which they termed ten planks. I have taken them off from the official record of that convention of which there is only one copy that I know of. That is in the parliamentary library and the librarian wants it to be handed back to him because it is the only copy and it is in demand. It may be that, not having seen this and having listened to what men like hon. gentlemen opposite have told them, there is an idea among the people, even among friends of the government, that we have proved recreant to the principles laid down at that convention. The first resolution had reference to the tariff. I intend to take that up later because I shall dwell longer upon it, as it is more particularly under discussion now. The second resolution was:
That the Liberal party is prepared to enter into negotiations with a view to obtaining a fair and liberal reciprocity, including a well-considered list of manufactured articles,

With the United States. Was that plank carried out? Certainly it was carried out. A man will write himself down ignorant of the history of his own time if he says it was not carried out. He knows that it was carried out and honestly carried out.
Explain?

Explain? Why the hon. gentleman does not need any explanation. He knows that representatives of the Canadian and United States governments sat first in Quebec, and subsequently in Washington and made every honest attempt to secure reciprocity. That they did not secure it does not mean that the plank was not carried out; the plank did not pledge them to secure it, it told them to try for it.
The third plank declared:
That the convention deplores the gross corruption in the management and expenditures of public moneys.
Was that carried out?

Yes, it was carried out at that time and that is the reason the resolution was put. It was a protest against the state of things then prevailing, and therefore that resolution was adopted and that resolution should be carried out. Whether hon. gentlemen say it has been or not, it should be carried out, and I claim it has been carried out.

In the same way as reciprocity, no change.
Mr. PATERSON'. \ Would hon, gentle-, men have any objection to replying to me when I have finished?
The fourth resolution read:
We cannot but view with alarm the large increase of the public debt and of the controllable annual expenditure of the Dominion, and the consequent undue taxation of the people under the governments that have been continuously in power since 1878, and we demand the strictest economv in the administration of the government of the country.
What are the facts?
Oh, oh.

They are evidently not cheering the facts but because I have not recited them yet. When this resolution was adopted great increases were being made to the public debt. The trade and commerce of the country was almost stagnant, public works were not being carried on. The Canadian Pacific Tailway was being built. While they were not collecting under the system of taxation they had in force enough money to pay the ordinary expenditures of the government, they

had to borrow, absolutely borrow money to meet the ordinary expenditures, without expending a dollar on public works or on capital account, and therefore it was that the public debt went up and up and up, till in their 18 years of power they had increased the public debt to $118,000,000 and odd, with nothing to show for it, for they had not carried on the public works. I mean nothing to amount to anything outside the Canadian Pacific railway. That resolution was adopted, but that resolution, you say, should be enforced by us. Deploring this evil in the late government have we fallen into the same mistake? Have we added to the public debt? Is there any cause for alarm in that respect now? As the Finance Minister points out to you, at the end of this present financial year, after 13 continuous vears in power, if you jleave out what has been borrowed on-the Transcontinental railway, a great national undertaking, we shall have paid all our other expenditures, ordinary and on capital account, running into the tens, yes the hundreds of millions of dollars, without adding a dollar to the public debt of the country. These are the facts. Why do hon. gentlemen opposite not cheer the facts? Thev are cheering the facts by contrasts. One hundred and eighteen million added to the public debt, and nothing to show for it, scarcely. Tens and tens, running into the hundreds of millions, expended on capital account, beyond the ordinary expenditure of this government, at the end of this financial year, outside the Transcontinental railway, and not a dollar added to the public debt. No cause for alarm now.

If the hon. gentleman desires to be perfectly fair, when he leaves out the expenditure on the Transcontinental, why does he not leave out the expenditure on the Canadian Pacific railway in making his comparison?
I alluded to the fact that the Canadian Pacific was being built. But what about all the other expenditures that we have made?

The increase of the public debt. I wish merely to say this, that the increase of the public debt included money to be spent on the Canadian Pacific railway in the one instance, and does not include the money borrowed to be spent on the Transcontinental in the other. Therefore, the comparison is not fair.

Oh yes, it is quite fair, the House well understands what the point is. We leave out both those undertakings. Take all that has been done by the Liberal government in digging canals, in bonuses upon iron and bonuses to railways, in all the directions in which we
have spent ten and tens of millions, running up to hundreds of millions more than those gentlemen spent on similar works, and we have done all that without adding a dollar to the public debt, while they had to borrow money for such works. Now I think that resolution has been carried out. We deplored, we viewed with alarm, the great increase in the public debt, and so we have endeavoured to keep it down, and we have succeeded admirably.
Resolution No. 5.-That it is the ancient and undoubted right of the House of Commons to inquire into all matters of public expenditure, and into all charges of misconduct in office against ministers of the Crown.
I am glad to hear that that is the principle on which both sides of the House agree, I am sure.
Resolution No. 6.-That in the opinion of this convention the sale of public lands of the Dominion should be to actual settlers only and not to speculators, upon reasonable terms of settlement, and in such areas as can be reasonably occupied and cultivated by the settler.
That plank was adopted-the very reverse of the policy that was being carried out by our Conservative friends when in power, and which we viewed as contrary to the well-being of the country. That plank we carried out, and every fair-minded man must say that it has been carried out in its entirety.
What about the land sold to the Robbins Irrigation Company?
Is that denied?
It is a fact.

A fact! Why, if any man wants to deny that these lands have been sold for the settler-talk as the hon member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) did about the Saskatchewan lands that were sold to these people! These lands were sold, but they were not sold in contradiction to that resolution, for they were sold with terms of settlement. Do you mean to tell me that that resolution was not carried out?
Yes, yes, no, no.

Then all I can say to you is this, that the united voices of 250,000 happily settled homesteaders give a denial to the statement. I take their word in preference to an objection of

Resolution No. 7.-The repeal of the Franchise Act, and that we should revert to the provincial franchise.
Was that carried out? Is that upon the statute-book now? No. Gentlemen may laugh, and try to be merry as they may, and deny it as bravely as they may, but they cannot say that that plank has not been carried out, because the Franchise Act has been wiped out.
May I ask the hon. gentleman a question? While we admit that it was carried into effect in 1898, did not the government try to reverse that action and adopt a Dominion franchise?

No, we did not. If I were to answer the hon. gentleman courteously, I say no, I say no; because my hon. friend alludes to the circumstance that took place in this House where there was a little question about the list in unorganized districts. That don't bear out what he says.
Not only in unorganized districts, but I think there was a a similar attempt made in British Columbia.

We wont enter into an argument on.that point.
Som hon. MEMBERS. Ha, ha, ha!

Really, they are the happiest lot of gentlemen in opposition that I have seen in a long time, rejoicing in the good times brought about largely through this government. No, Sir, that plank has been carried out.
Resolution No. 8.-To make the House of Commons a fair exponent of public opinion, and to preserve the historic continuity of counties, it is desirable that the conformation of the electoral division county boundaries should be preserved, so that in no case parts of different counties should be put in one electoral division.
Has that been carried out? Certainly it was carried out. A redistribution measure was _ brought in, and that resolution was carried out. You know that county boundaries were respected, you know that there was no gerrymander by this government, there was a perfectly fair division of these counties. And yet hon. gentlemen say we have not carried out any of the planks of our platform. There it stands. The counties are before their eyes, their own coun ties are there, and many of those gentlemen opposite know that the counties they now represent are within county bounds, and are not the same counties represented by their predecessors, when there were parts of two or three different counties thrown together in order to give a majority to one party against the other.
What had the government to do with that? Were not the electoral divisions fixed by a committee of this House?

I believe they were, and my hon. friend I think was on that committee. But that just shows the superiority of our redistribution. When the gerrymander was put through in 1882 by Sir John A. Macdonald's government, was it not done in secret? A committee of their own met in a room, a dark room, and there, Mr. PATERSON.
in secret, unknown, the men they were attacking, every Liberal that had been prominent in the fight in the House against them, was marked out for political destruction by these men, by virtue of an Act of parliament that they were getting passed with their majority. David Mills, one of the ablest men in this country, was singled out for political slaughter. Alexander Mackenzie-I leave myself out, though there was not a more infamous cut up anywhere in the Dominion than there was in my county;-John Charlton, Thomas Bain, and many others. Men who had been fighting them for the rights and liberties of the people of this country were marked out for political destruction by a committee that met in secret-marked out to be slaughtered by Act of parliament. And this was carried into effect so far as the decision of a majority in this House could carry it into effect. Let me illustrate by my own riding. They took from my riding two Liberal townships, giving majorities totalling three or four hundred, and threw them into South Oxford, where, even without them, there was a Liberal majority of six hundred. Then they took from another riding a Tory township and put it into mine. Thus they sought to put me, politically speaking, to death. And one thing that kind of makes me have a warm side for my Tory friends- or many of them-is that, while their friends in this House did that infamous act, there were men on the Conservative side in that riding who said: ' This is not fair play, and wo will not stand it; we will vote for the man you are trying to kill.' And they did. And so some of us got back-some of us did not. And now my hon. friend (Mr. John Haggart), in the innocence of his heart, asks if that is the way that the Redistribution Bill that we passed was prepared. And he was on the committee with some of his colleagues; the work was done in open daylight, with arguments heard, and a unanimous decision was reached as to what was fair and desirable. And now he thinks the opposition ought to have credit for jt.

As the hon. gentleman (Mr. Paterson) appeals to me, may I ask him to point out the distinction between the Bills that we passed and the ones passed under the government of Sir Oliver Mowat in Ontario?
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Haggart) wants to lead me on to a subject that is not under discussion.
Oh, oh.

There they are again. Can you, Mr. Speaker, see the appropriateness of that laugh? We are discussing the legislation of the Dominion parliament. And the hon. gentleman wants me to agree

that the credit for the Redistribution Bill passed under the leadership of the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) should go not to the government, but to the opposition.
I would like to ask the hon. member (Mr. Paterson) if he can show anything more shameful in the Act of 1882 than the gerrymander of Central York by the Liberal party of 1903?
I refer the hon. member (Mr. Wallace) to the hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. Haggart)for an answer. That hon. gentleman says that the Bill was a fair one and that they prepared it.
The member for South Lanark was overpowered by superior numbers in the committee.
Why, the committee were unanimous. ,
May I ask a question?

I would like to answer the hon. member's (Mr. Hughes') question, as he is so courteous, but I think it would be better to wait. The point is that we laid down the rule that county boundaries should not be disturbed; and, though there was the temptation to Tetum upon the heads of hon. members opposite that which they had visited upon us, Sir Wilfrid refused to act upon such an idea, but carried out literally and absolutely this plank of the platform.
Now, may I ask a question?
Yes.
Will the hon. minister give the population of West Northumberland and also the population of Victoria and Haliburton to show how the principle of representation by population is carried out?
I have not those figures. But I would ask the hon. member was not the rearrangement of the riding he represents fair to him?
The rearrangement made no difference to me
Was it fair?

The hon. gentleman has asked me a question; I will answer it in my own way. The rearrangement made no difference to me; I would have been returned no matter how the county was gerrymandered, and no matter whether it was made into one or two ridings. But the hon. gentleman opposite could not have done better in order to produce a split in the Conservative party than to gerrymander Victoria and Haliburton as they did in the last revision.
But will the hon. member say that he was not satisfied with the arrangement at the time?
The evidence before the committee will show that I fought for two ridings.
But I am speaking of one riding.
But there were two in Victoria and Haliburton formerly. I fought for two; I stood in this House alone in favour of two ridings in Victoria and Haliburton.

I know that the Bill went through with very little discussion, and that it was- admitted, even by Conservative newspapers, to be eminently fair. And it carried out the resolution of the convention in favour of maintaining county boundaries. I come to the ninth resolution. The first I have yet to speak about. But here are seven which, it cannot be denied, have been carried out. The ninth resolution has not been carried out. It is a difficult question. I do not know that the views of the Liberal party have changed concerning this resolution that there should be some change in the constitution of our Senate to bring it more into harmony with representative institutions? But the debate and vote yesterday, together with all that has transpired since this resolution was passed, go to show the difficulties with which this question is hedged about. They go to show that though this resolution is desirable in itself, as it was then in the eyes of the Liberal party, and apparently is now in the eyes of many of our Conservative friends, yet it has not been possible to carry it into effect. But there has been an honest desire to do it. Still, here is one resolution that has not been carried out.
Now, I come to the tenth and last resolution. At the convention, so far as I remember, there was no objection on the part of any one to anv of the resolutions save this. Let me read it:
That whereas public attention is at present much directed to the consideration of the admittedly great evils of intemperance, it is desirable that the mind of the people should he clearly ascertained on the question of prohibition by means of a Dominion plebiscite.
I say, objection was taken to that resolution. The [DOT] late Speaker Anglin voiced that objection and declared that he would not be bound by the resolution. Nevertheless, the resolution prevailed, and so became one of the planks in the platform of the party, making it incumbent upon the Liberal government to give effect to it, notwithstanding that some of the members of the party might not agree. And what was

done? You know that the plank was carried out and that the plebiscite was held in its entirety. So, these planks of our platform have been carried out in as fair and honest a manner as could be desired by the Liberal government elected on the platform of which tnese were planks. _ Now, I have read these resolutions which, in the opinion of hon. members opposite, if I am to judge by their scornful laughter, we have not carried out. But I think that fair-minded people, considering these resolutions and considering the action taken with regard to these matters by the present government, will say hereafter that if any man in this House or out of it declares that this government has been recreant to the resolutions of the Liberal convention, he is to be held as one sinning against the light, and as guilty of that of which no public man should be guilty- stating that which is not true of his opponents.
Now, I come back to the first resolution, and there is where our friends on the opposite side have time and again denied that we have carried out our platform in reference to the tariff. They say that the platform of the Liberal party at that convention was a platform of free trade as it is in England. Nothing harped on more, no statement made oftener than that, no statement more untrue-I was going to say- than that statement. I have that resolution. What is it? Is it a resolution for free trade as they have it in England-free trade and direct taxation, free imports .of goods into this country? Was that the policy? No. Here is the sense of it:
That the customs tariff of the Dominion should be based, not as it is now, upon the protective principle, but upon the requirements of the public service; .... that the highest interests of Canada demand a removal of this obstacle to our country's progress by the adoption of a sound fiscal policy, which, while not doing injustice to any class, will promote domestic and foreign trade, and hasten the return of prosperity to our people.
Here is the affirming part of it:
That to that end, the tariff should be reduced to the needs of honest, economical and efficient government. That it should be sp adjusted as^ to make free, or bear as lightly as possible, upon the necessaries of life, and should be so arranged as to promote freer trade with the whole world, more particularly with Great Britain and the united States.
.Is there anything in that resolution instructing a Liberal government, when it *came into power, to depart from the principle c>f indirect taxation and to adopt the principle of direct taxation? Nothing of the kind. A tariff is spoken of, a customs tariff is to be maintained and the revenues re to be raised by a customs tariff. There M. PATERSON.

There may be different views, but I want to tell you that these bounties came to be raised to what they are because we lowered the tariff on iron and steel, and it was made up in that way. We were enabled to reduce the duties on these articles through the bounty and the reduction of these duties meant a reduction in the raw material to the men who make the implements the farmer uses and to the industries in which iron is used, and in that way we have got the benefit. Just in passing let me say, because I am not going_ to argue or enter into a discussion of this question to-day, that we certainly do not give bonuses just for the fun of the thing.
I might remind you of another statement that the Prime Minister made in speaking of that policy. He said that we were to lower the rate of taxation and we were to do this without doing injustice to any classes. He emphasized that in the speech which he made by saying that when duties have been in force once it is not a very easy matter to reduce them because new industries have sprung up, but when you want to reduce them it ought to be done with great consideration and he was sure that when the Liberal government came into power they woulcl, not be indifferent to that primary truth.' We found the iron and steel industries in existence and the duties that were upon their products under the tariff of protection was $4 on pig iron and $10 on steel. We reduced the duty on pig iron to $2.50 and the duty on steel to $7. If we had done that without giving them increased bounties we should have done the injustice to them that was pointed out by the Prime Minister when he spoke at that time. That was our reason for doing this and it has been done. Now then if the steel and iron bounties, or any other bounties, are given for the advantage of some individuals alone, and have no national importance, they cannot be justified. That is the test that must be applied. If you give bounties they must" rest on the principle of the national importance of in-

dustry. We may differ in our views on this point, but I hold that these industries are of national importance. I hold that they are of -such great benefit, so widespread in their ramifications, that the whole country is benefited by these industries being in existence. I was struck when I was at Sault Ste. Marie by a statement which was made by one of the gentlemen who was connected with an institution there. I did not undertake to verify it, it may be an extravagant statement-I cannot say-but it struck me as an extraordinary statement when he told me that that industry located at the Sault employed more shipping tonnage than all the tonnage employed on the inland waters in moving the whole crop of the Northwest down to the ports of exit. I have not verified it, but it gives an idea of what strength there is in this. Perhaps the same cannot toe said of the oil industry, but at all events it was an industry whi'ch had been kept in existence by all the governments from -confederation down, and in order to lessen the duties which were paid toy our people on this article of prime necessity in the rural parts of the country especially, the duty was reduced and the oil producer was compensated by a bounty. The lead industry was the same. Cheaper transport for our products through improvements of our harbours: Montreal, Toronto, Fort William, Port Arthur, Port Col-borne, St. John, Halifax, Quebec and our lake and open ports generally; (6) enlarged canals and free canals; (7) improvement of the St. Lawrence river route; (8) cheaper transport on ocean steamers through a bonus; (9) cheaper transport through aid to railways toy bonus; (10) the -Crowsnest Pass railway through a bonus; (11) the Transcontinental railway through local expenditure and guarantee; (12) the South African expenditure (a direct expenditure); (13) the place we -occupy to-day in the thoughts of other nations. These are assets; these are all contributing sources to the magnificent prosperity we have in the country now. Why, Sir, the sending of these volunteers to South Africa raised high the fame of Canada. That is an asset and though it may not be direct it has been of vast indirect benefit to the country. Why did we improve the St. Lawrence route, and why did we enlarge the harbour of Montreal? I represent a rural constituency in part, and we are 400 miles from Montreal and several hundred miles further from the mouth of the St. Lawrence, but I am voting to -deepen and to light and to buoy the St. Lawrence river and to enlarge the harbour of Montreal. Is it because I like the people of Montreal better than I like my own constituents? Certainly not. Is it that for the pleasure of the thing I vote to spend millions of money, some of which was contributed toy my rural constituents, to im-67	'
prove our navigation facilities? No. Why is it then? It is -because, as I have often told my people and they agree with me, I want the harbour of Montreal enlarged because I want more ships to come to that port. 1 want more ships because the more ships the keener the -competition for cargo, and the keener the competition the lower the ocean freight rate, and because every cent reduction in the cost of transportation is a cent in the pocket of the producer. Who can tell the amount of permanent benefit that has -come to the farmers of this country from the expenditures we have made on the harbour of -Montreal and the improvement of the St. Lawrence? That route has been made so safe that ocean liners can come up there through the dark hours of the night as well as in the daylight. Time has been saved, risk has been lessened and freight has been lowered to the consequent profit of the producers of our exports. That is an improvement which is paying good interest on the investment t-o all the people of Canada. And so with the improvement of the harbours on the lakes: Fort William, Port Arthur, Midland, Victoria Harbour, Goderich and all these. That work is not done for the benefit of the people living in the locality alone; it is done to reduce the cost of transportation and, I say it here that if there is any benefit to be given to the agriculturist by way of lowering the tariff, just and equitable, the agriculturist is entitled to it. But, I hold that more can toe done to benefit the agriculturist of Canada toy reducing to him the cost of getting his goods in the market than by a reduction of the tariff. A reduction in the tariff is all right so far as you can go, but the farmer is vastly more' interested in the wise expenditure of all the money that comes into the public treasury, contributed by all classes as well as by himself, in bettering the facilities for transport aqd cheapening its cost. If by improving our transportation facilities we can reduce by two or three cents a bushel the cost of landing produce in the -consuming market, fancy what a benefit that is to the producer in the west, not only on one year's crop but on the crop of every succeeding year. Take, for example, the $3,360,000, contributed to the treasury by all the people of Canada, which this government gave to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to touild 330 miles of a railway from Lethbridge to Nelson. Our opponents spoke of it as the Crowsnest deal or the. Crowsnest steal, and they tried to magnify it into a scandal although I notice that this year they have dropped it. They do not refer to it any longer. There was an expenditure of some millions, concerning which the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) asked what had we accomplished by it. What did we accomplish? Sir, we secured the building of that



road. We have had a tract of 330 miles of undeveloped country opened up, in which there are towns, cities and villages and a mining population, producing wealth, adding revenue to the treasury by the taxation they pay. But that is not all there is in that bargain. One of the conditions on which we paid that $3,300,000 was that the Canadian Pacific railway was to give us
50,000	acres of coal land which they had acquired from the British Columbia government. That is our national asset to-day; and the fact that we have fixed $2 as the maximum price of the coal that may be sold there, is of untold benefit to the people who have to buy coal in the Northwest. That alone is an item which would justify the transaction. But what more did we do? It will be remembered that in the bargain made by the old government, the Canadian Pacific railway were not obliged to reduce their rates until their road earned 10 per cent net. Well, Sir, that was a contingency very unlikely to happen, and therefore this government, when they made the bargain with the Canadian Pacific railway to give them $3,300,000 to build that road, stipulated for a reduction in the freight rates on their whole system. By that means, we obtained a reduction which we could not have got otherwise. Among other reductions in freight rates, was a reduction of three cents per 100 pounds on all grain coming out of that country. What did that amount to? Figure it out, and you will find that the farmers, within four years, got back the whole of that $3,300,000, and they are reaping a proportionate and like benefit until this day and will be for all time to come. And yet we are asked in what manner we have promoted the prosperity of this country.
Might I ask a question? How many bushels of wheat are freighted over the Crowsnest Pass road which the hon. minister is speaking of?
The reduction I speak of applies to the whole system.
Has any wheat ever been freighted over that road?
No, but there has been wheat freighted over the other portions of the Canadian Pacific railway system.
I thought the hon. gentleman was speaking of the Crowsnest Pass road and of the expenditure on it.
There has been no wheat freighted over that road.
Then I do not see where the minister's argumenf~comes in.

That is because you did not rightly grasp the bargain. Under Mr. PATERSON.
that bargain, grain all over the Northwest territory which comes out on the Canadian Pacific railway system is carried at a reduced rate. If there be 40,000,000 carried on the Canadian Pacific railroad, that is carried at the three cents per 100 pounds reduction. Just think of it. The direct recipients are the men who grow the grain. It might be said that in fairness some of that money ought to have gone into the public treasury, but the farmers are the ones who get it directly. When they come to market their wheat, the buyer knows the ultimate price in the market'to which the wheat is going. He has to figure the freight and insurance charges and all the other expenses in order that he may know what margin there will be for him and what price he can afford to pay. And when he knows that he gets a reduction of 3 cents a hundred pounds on the freight, he is able to give the farmer the benefit of that at once, and it goes at once into the farmer's pocket because he gets it in the extra price which the wheat buyer is enabled to pay him. What does that mean to the people in the Northwest? While I do not undervalue their request for a lower tariff, what is that in comparison with the benefit they can derive from the wise expenditure of. money out of the public treasury to which all the people in the country contribute? It means millions. Whenever you can lower the insurance or the freight rates by deepening the St. Lawrence, by lighting it, by enlarging the harbours-every time you can take a cent off the cost of the transportation of the produce of this country, that is a benefit to the men who raise the crops. While I give every credit to my hon. colleague the Minister of Agriculture, for the steps he has taken and is still taking, in order to benefit the producers of this country, that is only a minor matter as compared with a wise expenditure of the public money in improving and cheapening the lines of transportation, and in this way giving our farmers money far in excess of what they would get had not these additional facilities been provided out of our public revenue. The great producing class of this country is the farmer, and therefore every reduction in freight is a reduction which goes into their pockets. More than half the total exports of this country are the products of the farm, so that the man who raises those products is the one who gets the benefit of the reduced rates secured to him by the expenditure of public money.

Might I ask another
question? Do I understand that owing to this legislation in reference to the Crowsnest Pass railway the freight rates on produce in the northwest were reduced three cents to the farmers?
Three cents a 100 pounds, yes.
This is the first time I understand that because it is not the case.
Then the hon. gentleman will be obliged to me for telling him.
For the information as it comes, but not for the fact.

I think my hon. friend will find it is correct. That was one of the conditions of the bargain made with the Canadian Pacific railway. We gave them $11,000 a mile for the building of 330 miles of railway. That was larger than any bonus given to any other company, the bonus generally being $3,200 a mile, and in some cases $6,400 through very difficult country. That subsidy was given not to build the road alone, but to secure to the people of the west the great boon of having a reduction in freight rates of three cents a hundred pounds for all time to come. In addition to that, lower rates were to be given on goods imported into that country, coal oil, agricultural implements, &c., so that, taking these things into consideration and remembering that the money has been paid back-although of course it went to farmers it was still paid back -and on that one item in four years there has been an immense relief to these people. I give it as an illustration of all the other expenditures. By wise expenditures of that kind you are benefiting the country, you increase your revenue, you have one of the greatest resources of the prosperity of this country. I have spoken at length. I do not apologize for it. I do not mean to say that I have spoken longer than I intended. _ When I rose I felt, whatever others might feel, that there were some things I wanted to say, things that in my judgment should be said, and I made up my mind I would take up as long as it required me if my physical force enabled my voice to reach your ears. I recognize the fact- that in the ordinary session, deducting the time devoted to routine proceedings, there is only between two and three hours of time for each member of this House to occupy the floor. I auite recognize that the large part of the time that might fairly be allotted to me has been consumed by me on this occasion and I therefore will endeavour to keep as quiet as possible during the remainder of this session.

natural resources than to their management of the finances of the country.
What position does my hon. friend take now in regard to Providence? Providence is surely at fault now. Under the Conservative government, Providence was doing -all the work. Now my hon. friend says, with his right hon. leader, that our prosperity and the wonderful progress this country has made are due to the wise policy of the Liberal party. Then my hon. friend touched upon a very interesting feature of the history of his party, the Liberal convention of 1893 at which he and some other hon. members on that side were present and the official report of which I hold in my hand. And this he did quite without any necessity, because I do not know that the subject has been raised in this debate. He takes upon himself'the somewhat onerous task of justifying the planks of that platform and of proving that each one of them has been kept by the party and not broken and disregarded. Well, Sir, there was a Liberal convention in Ottawa in [DOT] 1893. These hon. gentlemen having been then about fifteen years out of office, and, hungering for the sweets of office, they desired a platform upon which they could come into power. And so they met in solemn council in Ottawa to provide means by which they could satisfy the electorate that they ought to be elected to office. They, apparently, did not meet with many disagreements as among themselves and they parted after expressing by suitable resolution confidence in the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) who now leads this House, and singing ' For he's a jolly good fellow.' I can only say that, especially with regard to carrying out this platform and the promises which he made at that convention and afterwards made in the province of Quebec and in the west, there never was a ' jollier fellow ' in the history of Canada. For, as a ' jollier,' the right hon. gentleman is most successful. In the art of * flim-flamming ' the electorate the right hon. gentleman is a past master as a 'jolly fellow.' The Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) forgot some things concerning the carrying out of the principles of that convention, especially with regard to free trade. By reading the records of the convention, he tried to show that what the right hon. Prime Minister meant was not free trade as they have it in England-that that never was promised by the Liberal party of Canada. He read a certain portion of the hon. member's (Sir Wilfrid Laurier's) speech declaring that he would apply the principle as nearly as he could to work out the beneficial results which he expected would flow from it. Either the Minister of Customs is losing his memory or he did not see fit, when he was going into ancient history, to tell the House all he knew about Mr. BOYCE.
the statements made by the present leader of the House on the principle of free trade. He forgot to tell us that all that the right hon. gentleman said on the subject of free trade was not said in the convention hall. The right hon. gentleman had to satisfy parties in the west, and people down by the sea, and manufacturers of Ontario, upon that question. Arguing the matter years after the event the Minister of Customs forgets what the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) himself cannot forget, and what he dare not and cannot deny-his own utterances to the people of Manitoba in the city of Winnipeg in 1895. Let us see what he said and compare that with his attitude as interpreted by the Minister of Customs. The right hon. gentleman has heard these words time and again, but it would be a pity should he forget them:
I come before you to-night to preach to you this new gospel of free trade. I denounce to you the policy of protection as bondage. Yes, bondage. And I refer to bondage in the same manner in which American slavery was bondage. Sir, our policy is freedom of trade such as exists in England, such as is practised in Great Britain. I propose that we should follow England's example and open our ports to the products of the world. In the city of Montreal, the Liberal party believes in free trade on broad lines such as exists in Great Britain, and upon that platform, exemplified as I have told you, the Liberal party will fight its next battle.
The Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) forgot that expression, as he forgot some other matters, one of which is very fresh in our memories. He forgot the very interesting debate upon the Senate which we had yesterday and on which, I believe, the hon. gentleman cast his vote. He will remember the words of Sir Oliver Mowat, chairman of the Liberal convention, and he will remember the speech made by the Bight Hon. Sir Bichard Cartwright on that occasion in which he said:
I think, Sir, we all agree

That is the great Liberal party of Canada agree.
I think, Sir, we all agree that the constitution of the Senate as it at present exists is a blot upon popular government and upon free institutions.
And there was a plank in the platform to reform the Senate and remove that blot upon popular government and free institutions. But what has the party of the hon. gentlemen opposite done to remove that blot? Time after time discussions have taken place in this House on the subject of reforming or ending the Senate. Has my hon. friend (Mr. Paterson) lifted up his sonorous voice in favour of making good

that plank of the platform of the Liberal party ? I do not think so. I certainly have never heard the hon. gentleman speak on that question before. The hon. gentleman dealt also with the question of expenditure. He says that the Liberal party promised at that convention that the extravagance which they said was rampant under the Conservative party then in power should be checked and that there should be economy, wise economy, in the expenditure of the people's money. Well, I think my hon. friend's memory must be equal to the task of remembering some of the instances in which that plank has been violated. I think he remembers several instances in which motions were made in this House, and matters were brought to the attention of the government, in which an unwise expenditure, a very dishonest expenditure was the subject of very severe criticism, sometimes defended by my hon. friend, sometimes allowed to go in tacit silence. But we can refer to one or two instances of unwise expenditures. We have been treated lately to an incident of unwise expenditure-I refer to the Sawdust wharf which has been mentioned this afternoon; and there are others which make up the history of the life of this government, with mentioning which I will not weary the House at this time. But this remains, that whereas, under the Conservative government there was economy of administration, there was an attempt made to keep those, who were handling the people's money down to the letter, of their duty, and to see that every dollar of money was employed in the proper channel, yet how has that been swept to the winds by this party who promised to see that every dollar of the people's money should be wisely, honestly and economically spent. I will just quote one instance that occurs to me. and that is an instance where an official of this government were not exactly, what one might call, living up to the letter of honesty, I refer to the case which was the subject of a resolution in this House two or three years ago, a case in which an employee of the Immigration Department of the government was convicted of stealing from a person with whom he came in contact as search officer. He was sentenced to a term in jail, he spent the term in jail, and when he was released, largely by the very wise, the paternal act of the Minister of the Interior, he was rewarded by being put back in the position, with his' salary raised, and the scope of his duties extended. That is an incident of how the Liberal party has carried out that plank in their platfrom.

What is the meaning of that clause? I do not see the promoter of that Bill in the House; neither do I see the chairman of the Banking and Commerce Committee. It seems to me that we have no one here to vouch for this _ Bill. Certainly, if we are going to proceed with the Bill the promoter of the Bill at least should be here. This, to my mind, is a very important Bill and one which I thought should not have passed the Banking and Commerce Committee. I know there are others of the same opinion as myself. We were not at all satisfied with it and before we proceed with this Bill I think we should have the promoter of the Bill, or the chairman of the committee, to explain what the various clauses mean and why the company is asking for them. Some very peculiar things came up in the Banking and Commerce Committee in regard to this Bill, and the House is entitled to a great deal more light on the Bill than what we are going to get to-night, in the absence of the two gentlemen who are especially interested in promoting the Bill. I do not know what the government thinks about it; the government is very weak to-night, very lame. We have no one here to take charge of government measures except the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham). He is usually in his place. I commend him for it. I wish I could commend some of the others for diligence just in the same way, but I am sorry to say I can not do it. I do not know whether they have gone down to tne city to take part in the election that is going on at the present time.
They have gone to the hockey match.

They have gone to the hockey match. Well, if it has come to this that ministers of the Crown, when important measures are before the House, have nothing better to do than attend a hockey match, I think we had better adjourn parliament until the hockey matches are all over.
I think I will send for the leader of the opposition.

I understand the leader of the opposition is very well oc-

cupied to-night and possibly my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals will find out on the 29th of this month that he is doing mighty good service. The leader of the opposition is a free commoner. He is not bound to be here every night. He has lieutenants to look after the interests of the opposition, but the government is always supposed to be here. Here is a Bill respecting the Canadian Pacific railway and I am glad to see the Minister of Railways and Canals in his place. Here is another respecting the Canadian Pacific railway. The minister is in his place to see to that also, but there is another Bill respecting trust and loan companies.
The Minister of Finance is here.

Just arrived in time to escape castigation. I am delighted to see him. The Finance Minister is one of those men against whom we can say very little for non-attendance. I commend the minister for it. You will find him here late and early attending to his duties. I never knew him to go away to a hockey match when important business was on hand and I think the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Talbot) was too fast when he informed us that the ministers of the Crown, except the Minister of Railways and Canals, had all gone off to the hockey match. I hope that before the committee rises the hon. member for Bellechasse will rise in his place and do the Minister of Finance the justice of saying that he made a mistake and that he was not well informed, as he is nearly every time.
It is quite true that I made a mistake, but I did not think that my hon. friend's swallowing powers were as good as they are.

If the hon. member for Bellechasse has anything worth swallowing he can depend upon it I will open my mouth. I am here to listen, I am here to take note of what is going on, I am here to watch legislation and if men are not here who ought to be here to attend to matters of this kind I am obliged to express my opinion of them. This is not the first time that I have prevented a Bill from going through simply because the promoters of the Bill and the chairman of the committee were not present. I feel very much like taking that stand to-night. I am not going to boast of my power because I may not have a sufficient number behind me if the government should choose to divide on the question and call upon their friends to put the measure through with or without consideration, but I believe the good sense of the minister will cause him to reflect and I say that the course which I have taken is I the proper one to pursue. I remember that ' Mr. HENDERSON.
on former occasions the Minister of Finance has agreed with me that it is a proper thing to object to a Private Bill going through when the chairman of the committee or the promoter of the Bill is not in his place. I feel like appealing to the Finance Minister to-night to support me and I am inclined to think that if I do he will be gracious enough to do it. He may go wrong sometimes, like the hon. gentleman (Mr. Paterson) who addressed us this afternoon for nearly two and a half hours, when he undertook to show that the ten planks in the platform of the Liberal party, as laid down in 1893, had all been carried out. I do not think the Minister of Finance would get up in his place and support the Minister of Customs in that. I think he would modify his language somewhat, but I think the Minister of Finance would support me in the contention I have raised that we should not proceed with this legislation in the absence of more information, the information that can only be given by the promoter of the Bill or the chairman of the committee that had it in charge. Now, I am going to appeal to the Minister of Finance if I have not taken the proper stand, if this is not the proper mode of procedure. This is a very important Bill, a Bill that passed through the committee, and I say now, and I appeal to the judgment of other members of the committee, that we were not satisfied at all. We had our doubts about the Bill in the Committee of Banking and Commerce and I am rather inclined to think that the Minister of Finance will give me some support in stopping the progress of this Bill until the men come in who have the right to vouch for it and whose duty it is to explain it. I appeal to the House to prevent this bad example being set. I ask the Minister of Finance who is leading the House this evening to assist me in not letting Bills go through in this way.

In justice to the chairman of the Banking and Commerce Committee it is only fair to say he is engaged at present at a meeting of the committee on the race track gambling Bill. He has been in that committee since seven o'clock and may be there until nine o'clock.
I just left the committee and I saw him there.
