House resumed the adjourned debate on the proposed motion of Mr. Fielding that the Speaker do now leave the chair for the House to go into Committee of the Whole to consider ways and means for raising a supply to be granted to His Majesty.

Mr. Speaker, when you left the chair I was commenting upon the somewhat extraordinary speech which the Minister of Customs treated the House to. I was referring to the contention which the hon. gentleman made with a great deal of vehemence, that the pledges of the Liberal convention of 1893 had all been honourably carried out by the Liberal government. I do not see the Minister of Customs in his place to-night, and probably the remark that some of the ministers had gone to the hockey match applies to him. I am sorry he is not present that I might remind him of the speech he made at that convention. The hon. gentleman spoke there, and the report tells us that he was received with loud and continuous applause and that he had to tell the people to keep quiet because even he could not make himself heard above the din. He spoke especially with reference to the trade policy of the Liberal party in support of the resolution denouncing the principle of protection as radically unsound and unjust to the masses of the people, and declaring that any tariff changes based on that principle must fail to afford any substantial relief from the burdens under which the country laboured.
I quote from the words of the Minister of Customs:
You have laid down and emphasized again the principle held by the Liberal party in this matter of trade and commerce, that in the levying of the taxes of the country, regard should be had only to the necessities of the revenue and that the government should not seek by tariff legislation to favour any particular class in the community. I say this is no new principle. A revenue tariff was in force when our late leader, Alexander Mackenzie, who has gone to his long rest, held the reins of power; and he and his government fell because he would not yield to the cry for a protective tariff. From that dav to this the Liberal party have not ceased to proclaim that they believed that it was not right or just that protection, as a principle, should be recognized by the government of the country, and that they believed that the duty of the government was to raise the necessary revenue to discharge the duties devolving upon the government and to leave the people free to work out their own destiny, giving no undue advantage to any one portion of the community over another. And to-day, Sir, you have embodied that principle in the resolution now before us.
So that the hon. gentleman's memory was slightly defective when he tried to make out that the tariff for this country was not a protective tariff. His colleague, the Minister of Finance, will not deny that it is. How does the hon. gentleman, the Minister of Customs, reconcile the language he used in supporting that resolution which formed one of the ten planks of the Liberal platform, with the remarks he made to-day and with the budget we are now de-

bating. In that language he said lie was -in favour of a tariff for revenue only, whereas to-day he is lauding to the skies what is a moderately protective tariff and a tariff in some respects a great deal too high to suit some hon. gentlemen opposite.
These are anomalies with regard to which the hon. gentleman was very weak, and it seemed to me he was rather gratified when he was interrupted, as the interruption gave him the opportunity to assume the semblance of wrath and some little time to consider how he could best square himself with his former professions.
My hon. friend spoke about another platform-the platform of prohibition. Did his party carry out their promise with regard to that platform? They passed a resolution on the question of prohibition. Did they carry out what they promised in their speeches on that resolution? We know what the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) said. He said that if his party were elected, it would carry prohibition if such a measure had a majority in the country. Well, a plebiscite was taken and there was a majority in favour of prohibition, what has my hon. friend to say now? These hon. gentlemen, who were so lavish in their professions, took on themselves the responsibility of saying that the majority in favour of prohibition was not large enough to carry such a measure into effect.
There is one feature of the hon. minister's (Mr. Paterson) speech to which I cannot help but refer as it touches the question of the franchise law. I have no intention of discussing the amendments made by this government during the session of 1908; but if there be any more striking evidence of the desire of this government to secure unfriir elections, to gag the majority of the people and prevent the will of,the electors from being known and acted on, than the amendments to the Franchise Act put through by this government in 1908, I should like to know where it is to be found. They were simply intended to put a muzzle on the voters in the constituencies of northern Ontario, and they stand to-day as a monument greatly to the discredit of this government. The Franchise Act in 1908 created new regulations for making votes which resulted in a most outrageous state of affairs. That state of affairs I shall not enter into now, because it will form the subject of another discussion, but the people resented that outrageous condition. The opening of the Printing Bureau on Sunday by order of the Secretary of State, the running of special trains at the expense of the government, and a large expense it was, to carry voters' lists and constables, and the mounting of polls out in the bush by constables-all these things testify to one of the greatest outrages ever committed against the electorate. In order to carry out an election

in the riding of western Algoma, in order to enable this government to secure a majority in that riding and in the riding of East Algoma, there was a special train run from Ottawa starting on a Sunday. The Printing Bureau was opened by order of the Secretary of State on Sunday in order to print those voters' lists and send them on that special train and give to the government candidates whatever advantages might thus be gained. That was one of the results of the working out of these splendid franchise amendments to which my hon. friend pledges his support. All I can say is that when the true facts of the working out of that Act are made known, my hon. friend and the Prime Minister will realize that what was said when that franchise amendment was before this House in 1908, had a great deal of truth in it, and this amendment did work an outrage on the rights of the people.
We are gratified- by the condition of affairs as shown by the speech of my hon. friend on the budget. We know that this is an era in which Canada is enjoying great prosperity, that our resources are being developed, that our coal and oil lands are being developed, and that our timber resources are growing, but no man in his sober senses-certainly not the Minister of Finance-will say that for all these good things we must thank the Liberal party. The Minister of Finance may say that the Liberal party have made the most of what Providence has so abundantly endowed the country with, but hi will not go as far as the Minister of Customs did and say that while, under Conservative rule, Providence was responsible entirely for what little prosperity he grudgingly admitted the country then enjoyed, the prosperity of these late years, our great wheat fields, our girand mineral resources, are due to the policy of this government.
We have heard from time to time of the expenditure and it struck me that the Minister of Finance in speaking was rather proud to be able to say that we had reached what he called the hundred million dollar mark. It seemed to strike a peculiar note, . rather a jarring note to any person who had heard the minister and his colleagues in days gone by denounce an expenditure of $40,000,000, aye $38,000,000, as not only extravagant but as a crime and a shame. Four million dollars, three million dollars less would be quite enough to carry on the government in this country. I shall not draw a sharp contrast between the condition of affairs when we had an expenditure of $38,000,000 and $40,000,000 and to-day, when we have reached what the Minister of Finance, very proudly calls the $100,000,000 mark, but I can certainly say some things with regard to the method of making expenditures of public money. Contemplating an expenditure of $100,000,000 per

annum one cannot but feel that there are expenditures which may have been greatly misdirected, and that the whole scheme of expenditure for public buildings and public improvements calls for the careful revision by the government in the interest of the public welfare. What is the position now with regard to public buildings? Is there any governmental or departmental arrangement whereby when a post office building is necessary for the public service in any part of Canada, the Postmaster General makes a requisition on the Minister of Public Works and the building is put up? No, Sir, the very last man to be considered when a post office is needed in a constituency is the Postmaster General and the very last consideration which is given to the question of the erection of that building is whether it is required for the public service and for the convenience of the public. We have many instances of that. The Minister of Public Works will not say that when a requisition is made for a post office building or a customs building he consults and acts on the endorsauon of the Postmaster General or the Minister of Customs nor does he refer to the post office returns at that point. Otherwise we would not find in the estimates such an outrageous amount as $25,000 for the erection of buildings in places with a postal revenue of $700. But the Minister of Public Works has a peculiar method of getting rid of this enormous expenditure of $100,000,000, a peculiar method of spending the peoples' money. As I understand it is the bounden duty of the minister as a trustee of the people of Canada to spend the money taken from the people of Canada by taxation in the interest of the people of Canada for their purposes and for their services. Does he do that, does he pretend to do that? Instance after instance has been quoted in this House where the hon. gentleman has not done that, I believe that it has been proved to his satisfaction in this House that he has not done it, yet the hon. gentleman makes no comment, he simply persists in that method and in that line of expenditure, flattering himself that in doing that he is winning over the majority of the people of Canada who can be effected in the different ridings by the expenditure of public money. May I ask when the Minister of Public Works took the right to spend government money on private property? When did he become vested with the power, without the consent of the owners or the exercise of the right of eminent domain, to improve another person's private property with the money of this government? My hon. friend possibly knows to what I refer. During the last election he was very busy with his appropriations in the riding of West Algoma for wharfs, &c., doing his best to curry favour by paying out of the peoples' money in
order to win the peoples' votes for the government candidate. I do not mind the hon. gentleman adopting that petty and miserable form of bribery in my riding; it suited him and I am sure there was not one vote in that riding which was affected by the expenditures he made in it, but I did resent his action when in fulfilment of a pre-election promise he appropriated $3,000 to alter, repair and generally improve a wharf which the government did not own, in which the government had absolutely no interest, and with respect to which the minister had no correspondence with the owners. This was a direct bid for votes, it was a payment for votes of the peoples' money for a work the profit of which went entirely to the benefit of private individuals. Does my hon. friend deny that? Does he state that the government had any interest in that wharf or in the approaches to it, that the government was ever requested by any one interested in the wharf or the approaches to expend that money upon that private property? No, I tell my hon. friend and he will not deny it that the Liberal candidate during or after the last Dominion election requested the Minister of Public Works to expend $3,000 upon that private property, and, docile in such matters, absolutely careless as to what the conditions are, wilfully ignorant and blinding his eyes to the fact that nobody had requested him to spend money on that private property, having no other reason than that he was asked to do it by the person holding the Liberal patronage in that riding and for the purpose of making, as he thought, a few votes by the expenditure of a few miserable dollars, filched from the chest of the people of Canada. There, Sir, is the grand, broad principle of economic expenditure of the peoples' money.

If I may be allowed for a moment: I have not the slightest idea of the property to which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Boyce) refers. If he would be good enough to name the place, I shall make it my duty to inquire into the circumstances. I may say, it is not the policy or practice of the department to spend money on private property-
I am glad the hon. minister (Mr. Pugsley) has said that. He says it is not the practice of the department-
Would the hon. gentleman please give a little further information. When was the work done?
Improvement and repairs. The hon. minister has an item in the estimates for it-$3,000.
Oh, no. I understood my hon. friend to make the statement that the work had been done-
I did not make that statement.

He said the work had been done by the government upon that wharf and wanted to know what warrant there was for spending the public money on private property. I can say to my hon. friend-and he ought to have known it -that, with regard to this wharf, no moneys have been expended upon it; and, knowing that, I think he ought not to have made the statement he made to the House.

I am in the judgment of the House: What I stated was that the minister had appropriated $3,000 for the purpose of repairs and additions to that wharf, and that he had made that appropriation simply at the request of the defeated Liberal candidate in the last election.

The hon. gentleman will pardon me again: He says that I have made an appropriation. Any appropriation must be consented to by parliament, and, before a single dollar will be expended upon the property the title must be acquired and vested in the Crown.

I will take the minister upon that statement. He is responsible for the public works. For what purpose does he put $3,000 in the estimates for a wharf in which, according to the language used in this House by myself, the govern-, ment had absolutely no interest?

Does my hon. friend not know that before the title to a property can be acquired, parliament must vote the money? Only after that is done are the necessary steps taken to acquire the property. Those steps will be taken, as they always are in such cases, before a single dollar is spent upon the property.

The hon. minister is getting still deeper in the mire. He is on, record in this matter, yet apparently he does not know it. He told us in this House that absolutely no negotiations had been entered into for the purpose of acquiring that wharf and that the government had no interest in it. And I have letters from the owners to the effect that they have not been approached by the minister, and, if they were, had no desire whatever to allow the minister to acquire any interest without their permission.
They will not be approached until parliament votes the money for the purpose.
For what purpose?

To acquire the property.
Mr. PUGSLEY
There is no vote for acquiring the property. That is where he has mistaken the proposition.
If the hon. gentleman knows what the minister intends better than the minister himself does, all right.
What the hon. minister proposes to do is to repair and add to property owned by private individuals without consulting those individuals. That is on record in 'Hansard'.
No such thing.

I regret that the hon. minister's recollection of what takes place in his department is so meagre. But I shall take occasion before I resume my seat to put before him his exact words in that connection. It is futile for the hon. minister to try to draw a red herring across the scent. That appropriation speaks for itself and his own language speaks for itself. There is an appropriation to prepare and add to a wharf, and there is his statement that that wharf is private property and that the government never had any interest in it. And here is one of the votes of item 148 of the estimates :
Kensington wharf-additions and repairs, $3,000.
Yesterday, my hon. friend was questioned and gave answer as follows:

1.	Is the Kensington wharf, near Desbarats, U est AJgoma, the property of the government of Canada? If so, when was it acquired, how much was paid for it, and from whom was it
purchased?
2.	How much land was conveyed with the wharf to the government?
3.	If the wharf was not purchased by the government, is . there any contract in writing between the owner thereof and the government with regard to the use of the same?

1 and 2. No.
3. No.
Is not that entirely correct?

Yes. There was an earlier question answered by my hon. friend. He stated that there had been no negotiations for the acquisition of that wharf. He stated also that the government engineer had reported, not that it was desirable to purchase _ the wharf, but that repairs and alterations to the wharf would cost $3,300. And he puts $3,000 in the estimates for repairs and additions to the wharf belonging to private parties who never asked for it, his only reason being, I venture to say, that the person who has the patronage of the riding as defeated '* Liberal candidate asked to have it put there

for political reasons-to influence votes. And for that reason the minister filched out of the appropriations, $3,000
Mr. Speaker, I call the hon. gentleman to order. I think your ruling would be that he must take back that expression.
I think that the expression ' filched ' is unparliamentary.
I bow to your ruling. Mr. Speaker.

I would call attention to this further:
Members may discuss various questions on a motion for the Speaker to leave the Chair, without movin'? any amendments thereto, a great latitude being' always allowed on such occasions; but they may not refer specifically to any vote which has passed or is about to be discussed in committee.
If this has been referred -to Committee of Supply, it cannot be referred to on this occasion.
Then, I will leave the Kensington wharf to the tender mercies of the Minister of Public Works.
I think the hon. member is tired of it himself.

By no means. These are refreshing instances, and I notice that they arise much more frequently during the hon. gentleman's term of administration. Let me refer to another item which assists in making up the expenditure of this country to the splendid total of a hundred millions. I refer to the dredging on the Nipigon river during 1908. That is such a beautiful transaction. In years gone by, there has been a great deal of comment on the method on which dredging contracts were let, especially dredging contracts on the Great Lakes. I do not know any more startling example of contracts being let for political purposes on the eve of an election, and at rates so wholly disproportionate to the value of the work, without advertising, without notice to the persons who receive _ the contracts, than the Nipigon dredging. I will only refer to it shortly. Just before the election of 1908, without a contract, my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works set the Great Lakes Dredging _ Company to work dredging out the Nipigon. I say without contract, because the contract was not signed until some time after they had been set to work. There were no advertisements for tenders for that work. My hon. friend, of course, will not deny that. The work was commenced on the 8th of September, 1908; no contract had been signed then. There was $57,459.45 paid between that and December, 1908. The price per cubic yard, scow measurement, of rock was $3, other materials. 45 cents. He says:
Q. Were tenders invited for the work?-A. Yes.'
Q. If so, bow many tenders were received, who was the successful tenderer, and was the contract awarded to the lowest tenderer?- A. There were no tenders ever invited for this work. There were tenders invited by public advertisement for other work which did not include the Nipigon dredging.
Later on, in answer to a subsequent question, my hon. friend said that after advertisements had been inserted it was noticed that the Nipigon work had been omitted from the advertisement, and he remedied that by sending a private intimation to certain dredging firms.
To all the dredging firms operating on the Great Lakes. That is my recollection of it.

Quite so. It was intended to include this. These are my hon. friend's words.
It was intended to include the name of Nipigon river in the advertisement calling for tenders for dredging required at Bow-manville, Green Shoals, Jack Fish bay, Leaf, New Castle, Rainy river and Spanish river, which was published in the newspapers between the 3rd and 17th July, 1908 (list of news]vipers annexed). But the name was inadvertently omitted, and, as soon as this was discovered, the following letter was sent to-
Giving the names of the firms.
The hon. gentleman says that the notice was sent only to certain firms; hadn't he better give the names?

If my hon. friend will allow me to finish the sentence, I will satisfy him. He says that notices were sent to such and such persons. The House will remember the answer my hon. friend made just now, that the notice was sent to all the firms. But it is a significant fact that no notice was sent to the Great Lakes Dredging Company, and their name is not included in the list of firms to whom notices were sent. But they got the contract just the same, and they got $58,000 paid during the election year, and they got 45 cents per cubic yard for digging out sand from Nipigon harbour, where the same firm only got nine cents in Port Arthur.
They did not got 45 cents per cubic yard, the hon. gentleman is entirely in error. That is 27 times too much.

For the same stuff in Port Arthur they got nine cents, the same firm, but without any notification, and on the eve of an election; without a contract, because they did not have a contract, they were set to work in such a hurry. They got 45 cents per cubic yard for sand; for other materials the rate in Port Arthur harbour, 9 cents, the same as the same firm got by public advertisement. That is a sample

among many. That firm has been paid now upon that work $107,650.83. That is a very small percentage of the splendid expenditure of $100,000,000 to which the Finance Minister refers-on the Nipigon river work alone, and most of it was paid, a good percentage of it was paid, just during the months in which there was so much need in that wide and sparsely settled country to convince the electors of the purity of the administration and of the progress of the party represented by the hon. member for Thunder bay and Rainy river (Mr. Con-mee.)
Now, Sir, I have heard my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works speak with reference to the necessities of a post office in the town of Steelton. I have heard him say in public that it was a necessity, and that it was very strongly urged. It is an important town. The revenue of the postal department and the requirements of the public service demand that such a building be erected. I say to my hon. friend now that he had better employ the public money in the commencement of a public building in Steelton, the town within the corporate limits of which are situated one of the greatest steel industries in Canada, rather than fritter away the money by repairing and altering, and improving other people's property. I give him that slight hint, and I hope he will take -it from me in the spirit in which it is given. I also suggest to him that he immediately take some of the money which he is squandering at the extravagant price of 45 cents per cubic yard in Nipigon harbour, paid to the Great Lakes Dredging Company, and build the rest of the post office at Steelton, and so give to the public there the service they stand sorely in need of, as the minister has been made aware of by petition and by deputation, and has substantially acknowledged the justice of the request. We have other examples of the splendid expenditure of $100,000,000, and some of them have been referred to in this House. There is no better example that occurs to me at the moment than the splendid waterway which in future will be a monument to the great progress, at any rate to the great expenditure, of this government, and that is the Newmarket canal. My hon. friend, I quite believe, concurs in the magnificent utility of that work, a work that must make this government a laughing stock to both Liberals and Conservatives alike.
Now, Sir, I desire to refer for a moment t ) the expenditure on the Militia Department, and I regret that the Minister of Militia is not in his place. An hon. gentleman suggests that he also has gone to the hockey match. But perhaps not. With regard to the Militia Department I have but little to say. The militia of Canada costs us $6,000,000 a year to maintain. About a Mr. BOYCE.
million dollars a year, in round figures, is expended for the upkeep of agriculture. A comparison is not very much to the credit of this government. There have been criticisms, Mr. Speaker, about the manner in which the Militia Department has been administered, and those who did venture to put their nose into the department and begin to lift lids and turn things up went and wrote down about it that it was top heavy, that there was too much expense at the top, that it was overpaid, and I think there was some suggestion made that there w-as need for reform. There is certainly need for some reform all along the line. The Minister of Militia was anxious to mimic the English system in regard to the government of that department, but it did not turn out as satisfactorily as he thought it would and the sooner he drops that system and gets down to some practical one, and one which will conduce to the best interests of the country, the better it will be. I speak feelingly upon this subject. I speak with a view to local considerations because it seems to me that it was a mockery that with this expenditure of $100,000,000 a year by the government and an expenditure of $6,000,000 a year for the militia, when the town of Sault Ste. Marie got into dire straits, when men were rioting, turning over street cars and committing disorders of that sort, it could not have the protection of the militia without being called upon to pay dearly for it. The militia was called out, they sent up these gilded gentlemen with their clanking swords and spurs, they paraded through the town, went through their little drills, came back to Ottawa a day or two afterwards and the department sent in a bin for $8,000. This government is now suing the town of Sault Ste. Marie to recover this sum for services that were absolutely required in defence of life and property and in a time of danger and emergency. It seems to be an extraordinary circumstance that the Militia Department can make regulations by which the already heavy burdens of the town of Sault Ste, Marie are made much more grievous by this claim which is made for policing the town in an emergency like that. It seems to me an extraordinary thing that when Canada is maintaining, at an expense of thousands of dollars a year, this Militia Department, a lot of gilded mummery, as far as I can see, disturbances, such as I refer to, cannot be quelled except at a rate per diem or at the rate which the government-claim from the town of Sault Ste. Marie, amounting in all to $8,000. What is the use of our paying for a police system if every time the policeman is sent out to discharge his duty there is an extra amount payable while he is at work over that which he is entitled to receive when he is idle? I earnestly hope that there will be some practical reform in this direction,

and that the whole of the department which, from the little experience I have had of it, seems to be greatly in need of reorganization, will be thoroughly investigated and reorganized. I believe that if these reforms are put into practice a better state of things will result.
The districts of northern Ontario from which I and some of my fellow members have the honour to come as representatives in this House, have developed tremendously during past years. As we know, since 1904, the construction of the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway has opened up tremendously rich deposits of gold and silver-more silver than gold up to date. The extension of the line has further developed the tremendous clay belt tributary to its junction with the main line of the Grand Trunx Pacific now under construction, and it will make a capital channel of communication when that road taps the Transcontinental. I should like to have seen the attitude of this government towards that railway a little more generous than it was. It is a railway that has abundantly given returns for its expense. I certainly think that this government, in view of the splendid purpose that it was to serve in the development of the country, might have given to that road the assistance which it was suggested at one time should be given. The Algbma Central railway, another railway which is projected to Hudson bay, will cross the Canadian Pacific railway, the Canadian Northern railway, when it is built across the continent, and the Grand Trunk Pacific and will reach Hudson Bay. The Bruce Mines and Algoma railway is another railway projected to Hudson bay and these two railways, as the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway, will run through a country which is rich in mineral and timber. The building and government assistance of these roads are very much to be wished for at an early date. With regard to the Algoma Central railway we have every assurance that within a short time it will be in connection with the main line of the Canadian Pacific railway. This leads me to make the comment that the prosperity of Ontario during the last, say five years, has greatly contributed to the coffers of this Dominion. I never heard hon. gentlemen during the last Ontario election say that the increased revenue of Ontario which flows from the natural resources of the country was due to the wise and economical management of these resources, but on the other hand they declared it to be simply a matter for which Providence was responsible, although they claimed that the growth and development of the resources under the jurisdiction of the Dominion government were due to the
economical manner in which they had been administered.
There was a reference in the speech of the Minister of Finance to the steel bounties, and I listened with a great deal of interest to what the hon. gentleman had to say. I know something about the history of these bounties as applied to the town of Sault Ste. Marie. I remember being in the town before the bounties were applied and I know something of the history of these industries. The steel works of Sault Ste. Marie are, I believe, second to none in Canada as far as their capacity and equipment are concerned. I believe their output is not the largest in Canada at the present time, although I am not sure about that. I think it is not as great as that of the Dominion Iron and Steel company, although it is growing almost daily under our present conditions. Some hon. gentlemen object very strongly to the paying of bounties to steel and iron industries. The subject, of course, is one upon which there is a great difference of opinion, and I have heard hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House express opinions against bounty-fed industries. But we have practical results up there from these industries and we have practical results from the stimulus given to iron and steel industries all over Canada. As far as I can see, both from theory and the practical results which I have seen, the granting of bounties on iron and steel has not been a detriment to the progress of Canada, but it has been a stimulus to the great -iron and steel industries as, I think, the returns, which I propose to refer to presently, will show.
My hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) who I am sorry is not in his seat, denounced bounties upon purely theoretical grounds and he quoted some noted political economists in support of his conten-tention. But political economists differ with regard to the bounty system, and where you find that without any drain on the people of Canada a great industry is started up, and prospering, and increasing almost daily under the encouragement of bounties, that is the best practical answer to the theories of the economists. However, I desire to deal with practical things and I shall not discuss theories with the member for Red Deer further than to quote for his information what Professor Marshall says with regard to bounties:
Principle of economics:-
It might even be for the advantage of the community that the government should levy taxes on commodities which obey the law of diminishing return, and spend ' part of the proceeds on bounties to commodities which obey the law of increasing return.
It is an undoubted fact that the ' steel and iron industries-I speak especially in

211&
regard to the Sault St. Marie industry has been the parent of minor industries; it has caused the increased importation of machinery which gives a large increase to the revenue; it has brought about general prosperity, increased the population and enabled the people to earn more and to buy more. That beneficial condition during the last two or three years is going to be enhanced greatly in the near future. The Algoma Steel Company which is a subsidiary company of the Lake Superior corporation has recently had invested in it a large amount of English capital and it contemplates great and immediate development. A new merchant mill with a capacity of 600 tons per day or more will be erected as also a new blast furnace, a number of open hearth furnaces and a cokeing plant. Six and a quarter million dollars of capital will be invested in that enterprise and that is no small matter to the country at large. The building of a new cokeing plant means that instead of bringing a train load of coke each day from the United States, the coal will be manufactured into coke at Sault Ste. Marie and the by-products, such as gas and tar, will be extracted and utilized, and employment will be given to 3,000 additional men. That work will now be done by Canadians who will utilize the resources of the country, and in future that money will not be sent to a foreign country to pay for the coke. But more than that, it means cheapened cost of the finished product and with an output of from 800 to
1,000	tons of steel rails per aay, 50 cents per ton less in the cost of production means a tremendous advance in the industry. The Sault St. Marie company realizes, as I think the country realizes that the day must come when the fostering care of bounties will be withdrawn, but for the present at all events I sincerely trust the Finance Minister will not reverse the policy of the government in granting bounties to the iron and steel industry. This is a critical time in the history of these industries; there are 5,000 or 6,000 people employed directly and indirectly in the enterprise and it is not an industry that can be created in a day. It has had a somewhat chequered career; it has had to contend with serious difficulties at the outset, and I can assure the Minister of Finance that it is only now that the dark cloud is being dispelled and that the company is getting on a solid basis. For the next two or three years that industry will need the stimulus which the bounties give and it is in the interest of all Canada that they should be continued. Let us see how the steel trade of Canada has grown in recent years. I do not want the Minister of Finance to understand that I am giving his government the credit for the Mr. BOYCE.
great growth that has resulted from the bounties on iron and steel.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would never suspect it.

Well, I can tell the hon. gentleman that I am frankly prepared to do him justice and to give him and his government the credit that I believe is due them. In that respect I might mention that the making of coke from soft coal is rendered a great deal cheaper bv the draw back included in the tariff of 1907. In 1881 the value of the products of iron and steel was $16,943,321; in 1891, it was $29,874,437; in 1901,	$34,878,402; and in
1906, $53,125,265. So that there has been a steady substantial growth in the steel products of Canada, and my hon. friend will see that the growth between 1881 and 1891 was much greater in proportion than the growth between 1891 and 1901.
Then with regard to the average production, according to the tables, each iron and steel worker produced in 1881 on an average $1,237 worth; in 1891, $1,365 worth, an increase of $128 per man; in 1901, $1,409 worth, an increase of $34 per man; and in' 1906, the average production per man amounted to $1,752. The bounties paid by the government upon steel alone during 1908 amounted to $1,019,201, and on pig iron to $863,819; and on the manufacture of steel to $347,135. The manufacture of pig iron is in itself a very important industry in this country. It gives employment to a very large number of men and keeps going a large number of subsidiary industries. The Lake Superior corporation is now putting in a plant for the manufacture of pig iron which will, when completed, furnish enough pig iron to caTry out its own work without having to import pigf iron from any other country or concern. We, therefore, look forward to the dajt when Canada will supply iron and steel for her own manufactures. There is the Dominion Iron and Steel Company in the east, and there are the Soo industries immediately on the great lines of transportation to the west which find a ready market for their products in the gTeat west. Therefore, I hope that durng this period of transition in which these plants are being strengthened, the government will be lenient, paternal and progressive with regard to these bounties upon steel and iron products.
Before I take my seat I must refer to a matter which is possibly the most important that has ever come before the Canadian people. I refer to that paragraph in the speech from the Throne regarding Canadian naval service. When the fathers of confederation met within these walls to lay the charter of this great commonwealth, there were many misgivings expressed as to the outcome of confederation. My hon.

friend the Minister of Finance had very great misgivings. They were so acute that he moved a resolution in Nova Scotia in 1884 asking that that province be taken out of the union and made into an independent province. One hon. gentleman in 1867 spoke with much trepidation about the defenseless condition of the country. He wanted to know how it was going to be protected against foes by land and sea, and he pointed to the large extent...of border that lay exposed to an attack from the country to the south of us and the immense coast line on the west, east and north absolutely undefended. Other hon. gentlemen, but to a lesser extent, expressed their apprehensions on this point, but there was an hon. gentleman on the government side in those days. Dr. Tupper, now Sir Charles Tupper, who gave a quiet, calm and dignified reply, to the effect that when this country was confederated it would not lose its status as an important colony of the British realm, it would not be divested of its allegiance to England, ibut would stand for everything British and imperial, and in .time of danger England would protect this country as she had always done and we had nothing whatever to fear. That was England's guarantee at that time. England stood by Canada in the days of her youth when Canada could not protect and provide for herself. We have since had occasion to face difficulties and crises, and on every occasion Canadians have emphasized their desire to stand by the mother country, have burned with indignation when she was insulted, have mourned with her when she mourned, and fought with her when she was attacked.
That has been the sentiment of Canada's sons, that has been the sentiment that dominates Canada. Canada from ocean to ocean from south to north, is exclusively and exceedingly loyal and nothing that Canada can do to cement the ties that bind her to the mother country, will, in my opinion, be left undone if the Canadian people are allowed to have their say. There has recently arisen an alarming condition in respect to war against England. We have not simply idle rumours, we do not bring to this House merely the talk of the man on the street, we are face to face with what we are_ told by the greatest authorities on that subject in the empire, and the British people have been warned by these authorities, that the day is not far distant-some one suggested twenty years, and Lord Roberts' reply was twenty months-when you will find a directly hostile attempt to question England's supremacy of the seas. Other statesmen have spoken on the same question and given the same warning. I notice that an American magazine recently sent to a writer to Germany to make a personal and critical examination of the conditions in Germany, to ascertain whether
the rumours with regard to the preparations there and her intention with regard to British supremacy had any foundation. The report made and published in the magazine was by no means re-assuring to the people of Great Britain. It was shown that Germany was, to the limit of her resources, building vessels of the highest class of efficiency whose only use could be that they should be placed in commission in the German ocean and the North , sea to challenge England's supremacy in that sea. I do not wish to refer to the subject matter of the Bill now before the House, but the question is what is Canada going to do in this matter? The Prime Minister proposed a policy of a Canadian naval service which will mean the gradual education of men for the navy, their enlistment and training so that they can take their place oil the ships which it is the policy of the right hon. gentleman to build. His reply to the call from the other side is that we shall start now to build a training school and gradually work up so that in fifteen or twenty years we will be in a position to meet the crisis which threatens us in twenty months. The right hon. gentleman's policy further is that Canada shall in the future build war vessels to defend our coasts; but when you contrast the class of vessel which the right hon. gentleman announces this government will construct with the vessels of foreign nations, you are struck by the fact that not only can these vessels not be put into commission in time to meet any such emergency as we are told is threatened, but when it is put in commission, it will not be useful at all as a fighting or defensive factor, because all of the proposed vessels together will not have power enough to meet one vessel of the type which the German empire are building as rapidly as they can. I feel very keenly the necessity of Canada at once doing something to emphasize her position in this matter. The position of the leader of the House is not an answer to the situation, there is no answer to the call for arms, no answer to the threat of danger, no answer to the threatened attack on England's supremacy of the seas in the proposal to establish a Canadian naval service. It is not a question of what the right hon. gentleman proposes to do-fifteen or twenty years from now-to defend the empire and cement the ties that bind us t,o the mother country; it is not to emphasize our allegiance fifteen years from now that the people of Canada are crying out. What the people of Canada want is to demonstrate here and now that Canada amongst the foremost nations of the earth, Canada in all her pristine strength, with her magnificent resources behind her, with her splendid expenditure of $100,000,000 of which the Finance Minister so proudly speaks, is able to do, must do, and will cheerfully do her



hon. friend and his party were making. On that occasion Sir John A. Macdonald concluded his eloquent speech by the memorable words: ' A British subject I was bom and a British subject I will die.' My right hon. friend, as leader of the opposition, came into this House, and in the debate on the address delivered himself in the words that I will quote, and I commend them to him in the light of some of his recent utterances:
Sir, I am free to admit, that I, for one, when I made up my mind in favour of this policy, looked up first and last to the interest of Canada, and not to the interest of England. I am a British subject and I never forgot it yet, but while I am a British subject I remember that I am also a Canadian and I sit in the Canadian parliament. Let the British subject who sits in the British parliament look after the interests of England. When this confederation was organized (and no one knows it better than the right honourable gentleman himself) it was organized with a view of forming a nation of this United Canada. The honourable gentleman must have foreseen, since this was to be a nation, that some day or other the interest of this young nation would come in conflict with the interest of the motherland.
The hon. gentleman further proceeds:
It is absurd to suppose that, situated as we are, the interest of Canada will always be identical with the interest of Great Britain. Some day must come when these interests will clash.
Well, Sir, I sincerely hope that the day has not come when, in the opinion of the right hon. gentleman, the interests of Canada clash with the interests of Great Britain upon so great, so vital a question as the protection of the empire. I cannot believe that the right hon. gentleman would yield to the application of any one of these sentences to the present crisis. But why does he not meet the situation, why does he not do something to satisfy the people of Canada that he is at least as ready as New Zealand and Australia, very much weaker parts of the British empire, to help the mother country? I do not wish to suggest that the right hon. gentleman is desirous of serving the exigencies of party politics. I sincerely hope that the right hon. gentleman will free himself from all those bans and stand free and broad and all powerful as representing the free Canada that is behind him on this subject. It he will only speak and speak now and express the same willingness that other less powerful colonies have done to do their part I am sure that he will not lack in that applause from the people of Canada which he loves so much to hear. On the general ground and having regard to the general scheme, I do not like the proposition that the right hon. gentleman makes at this juncture in regard to the creation Mr. BOYCE.
and organization of a Canadian navy service. I do not like it. I do not think that it will redound to the credit of Canada. I do not think it is an answer to the question that Canada is called upon to answer I think, and I say it with much respect, that the right hon. gentleman is evading that question and I hope he will recover from his indisposition to speak and that he will speak to the issue and speak freely and clearly. This proposition will not raise Canada's reputation in the eyes of the world. It will not give to Britain's foes that greater respect which otherwise they would have had if Canada had taken, or if she would now take, a different stand. It will not strengthen the loyalty of Canada's sons, it will not strengthen the ties which bind us to the motherland, but there is the crying danger that it will serve political expediency and that it will shelve a very difficult question and one which the right hon. gentleman in times past has shown reluctance to face. It will satisfy some wavering followers who do not like to touch questions such as this and who would be better satisfied by a policy of masterly inactivity rather than bv a policy of instant activity. It will provide in its working out a great many public works in constituencies where they will be most useful and it will provide for patronage and all the other public evils from which this countrv has suffered under this administration. These are greater questions even than the question of supply and demand, than the question of revenue and expenditure, than the question of an expenditure which has reached the hundred million dollar mark. This is a question as to what is going to be done, a question of the duty of the _ moment, a question of whether Canada is going to face that duty, or whether Canada is not going to face it and it is not a question that the people, to whom this government has to answer, will allow the government to drop whenever they have an opportunity of passing upon that subject. In 1908 there was a "brilliant spectacle in the old city of Quebec, the tercentenary, marking a very important epoch in our history and one in which we all gladly joined. The Prince of Wales as the heir apparent of the British Throne, was there, it was a brilliant assemblage, it was a magnificent scene and a splendid page of history was written for Canada. But of what avail was all that display of loyalty? Of what avail were all those professions at that time, when after the tumult and shouting die, when the captains and kings have departed and when we are face to face, as it were, with wars and rumours of wars, there is absolutely nothing done or nothing suggested that should be done to meet the emergency which may be imminent, or which, as I fervently hope and pray, may be far off.	_

Is it not enough that it is threatened, is it not enough that it has been the subject of grave fears and alarm in England? Is it riot enough that the people of this country are satisfied that something should be done? I cannot help tout refer to a speech that was made in this House very recently by the hon. member for Hochelaga (Mr. Rivet) which contains a very remarkable paragraph upon this very question. The hon. gentleman does not give to the House any information as to his own views upon this subject. He is content with hurling criticisms and snarling at the position of the opposition in regard to it and hoping that the position of the opposition will be as he prognosticates. He says:
I have good reason to fear that the opposition are preparing to raise prejudices in the province of Quebec against this government, and more particularly against its leader, in the coming election, on this very question of naval defence. The Liberal administration and its faithful supporters will be charged with having been traitors to the interests of Canada at large, and particularly with having betrayed the interests of the French Canadians of the province of Quebec. On the other hand, I perceive the argument they will use in some of the other provinces. They will contend that the present government have not gone far enough in their policy of naval defence, and that because the government has not adopted a policy directly opposed to the wishes of the Conservative party in Quebec, it should be driven out of power as unworthy of the confidence of the Canadian electorate.
What does that mean? It' means that my hon. friend is constituting himself a prophet and that he is himself raising the ground work for a quarrel that I am constrained to believe he dearly wishes would come along so as to enable him to protect himself and to give argument for the position which possibly he will desire to take later on. I desire to express tire hope that the inactivity upon this question of the Prime Minister will not satisfy the Canadian people and will not satisfy the world. I will quote from a poem which has recently been placed in my hands upon the question of a Canadian navy which appears to contain some truth with reference to the situation as it is before the public to-day. I quote this, not because I think this House is fond or hearing poetry, but as an indication of what the Canadian people are feeling and expressing upon this question of instant and immediate assistance being rendered and being effective and ready in case of the emergency with which we have been threatened.
O, for a Man! to stand for us within our Council Hall,
With good red blood in heart and veins-and answer England's call!
To cut the Party questions from This Question all should feel,

Sir, there is a sentiment in that verse which demonstrates the growing sentiment and perhaps the dominating sentiment of the people of Canada. I gladly place it on record because I feel it contains much with which the people of Canada are strongly in sympathy. I believe, Sir, that Canada will stand firm to the empire. I-believe, Sir, the day will never come when the Canadian people will shrink from doing their duty towards the empire. In all her strength and in all her pristine magnificence Canada can do much, and Canadian prestige can do piuch to stop this war of construction. If Canada as the right hand of England, if Canadians as the sons of England were to come forward and say: We are heart and soul with the motherland in this crisis and a challenge of her supremacy of the sea is a challenge to Canada, what a powerful effect that would have upon the situation. Canada's sons are ready to-day as they always have been ready to answer to the call of the empire, if call there should be, which God forbid, I tell you Sir, that if that crisis ever arises there will be no room for questions of diplomacy, for sunny smiles, for sympathetic words, for motives of political expediency to hold the Canadian people from doing their duty and their full duty and their instant duty to rush to the assistance of the motherland. Only by that magnificent sympathy and only by that great prestige shall the British empire maintain herself and expand and progress with Canada in the front rank; Canada with all her resources, in all her magnificence, in all her wealth; Canada increasing year by year in population and resources, Canada the most important factor in the British empire, in her strength, in her power and in her ability to serve and fight for the empire, demonstrating the truth of the words:
Wider still and wider shall thy hounds he set,

Mr. Speaker, at this late stage of the debate, it is not my intention to take up at any length of the time of the House. I shall deal particularly with the question of the adverse balance of trade which our friends on the other side have had so much to say about in the debate. But before entering on that subject let me refer to some of the criticisms which have been offered on the naval policy of the government, not only by the hon. member (Sr. Boyce) but by my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle (Mr. Lake) who I am sorry is not present tonight. That hon. gentleman (Mr. Lake) made the statement that it was proposed to spend the miserable pittance of something like $2,700,000 a year on the navy Had he listened attentively to the speech of the Prime Minister he would have known that it is proposed during the next two or three years to build a unit which if built in England will cost $11,000,000 and if built in Canada 33 per cent more or $15,000,000 and which will cost about $3,000,000 for its upkeep on the English basis, and possibly $5,000,000 a year in Canada. There is an expenditure of $15,000,000 to start with and an additional expenditure of $5,000,000 a year, and yet the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lake) says that the government proposes only spending $2,700,000 on the navy. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Lake) also toid us that he was ashamed to acknowledge that he was a Canadian, and he said that we were sponging on the mother country and would likely sponge on her as long as she would allow us. Well Sir, I am sorry to think that any Canadian is ashamed to call himself a Canadian. We on this side of the House are proud to call ourselves Canadians and we stand as one man for the proposal of the right hon. the Prime Minister in connection with the Canadian navy. Every man on this side of the house bar none, is heartily in favour of the proposition made by our right hon. leader. Can the gentlemen on the other side of the House say as much? No. If the member from Qu'Appelle has anything to be ashamed of at all he should be ashamed of belonging to a party that does not know where it stands on this question. The leader of the opposition is the only man on ..that side of the House who has'taken a pretty decent course on this question and he has supported the resolution which was passed last year and is doing his best to stand by it, but his followers will not stay by him. The other day we had the spectacle of the leader of the opposition making one proposition and then his lieutenant getting up and making a proposition diametrically opposite, and then a supporter from Nova Scotia getting up and making, a third proposition.

My hon. friend from Qu'Appelle (Mr Lake) would have us believe that the party opposite are ready to do ever _ so much for the empire. Let me remind him that his party were in power prior to 1896, and I defy him to point to anything they ever did on behalf of British connection or any assistance they ever rendered the British government in any British war. Did they ever organize and pay a contingent to go over and fight the battles of the empire? No, it remained for this government to do everything practically that has been done to better the conditions between Canada and England and strengthen the connection between the two. Who was it sent over the first contingent? It was this government. Who was it that relieved the British taxpayer from the expense of keeping up the forts of Halifax and Esquimalt? Hon. gentlemen opposite, when they were in office prior to 1896, had the opportunity of doing the same thing. Did they ever suggest anything of the kind? Never. Who gave a preference to British goods in the Canadian market? It was the Liberal party. Who now comes forward with a proposition to spend millions of dollars on the building of a navy and its maintenance? It is this government. Therefore, it comes with very bad grace from hon. gentlemen opposite to make the criticisms they have made and such as we have had from the hon. gentleman who preceded me (Mr. Boyce). He took up some two hours and a half repeating for the most part the speech he has already made every session during the past four or five years. He criticised in a general way the expenditure of the Finance Minister, -but when the expenditure in his own constituency was in question, he came forward with a whine and asked that it be continued and that millions of dollars a year should still be paid out as bounties on iron and steel. I cannot agree with him. I do not propose to discuss what good has been accomplished by the $15,000,000 or $18,000,000 we have paid out in bounties on the production of iron and steel. I listened with great attention to my hon. friend the Minister of Finance when he referred to that question in his budget speech, and I trust that these bounties have had the good effect he says they have had, but taking that for granted, these establishments are now in a very flourishing condition, they are making a great deal of money, their stocks are above par, and their watered stock, which represents nothing at all, is selling at a market value of tens of millions of dollars. In the face of that condition, I trust the Minister of Finance will turn a deaf ear to the hon. member from East Algoma who asked that these bounties be continued. There is this further to be said. If these bounties were being used for the development of Cana-

dian mines and ores, they would not be so objectionable, but for one ton of Canadian ore that is smelted, there are many tons of foreign ore. Practically the whole output comes from foreign ores, so that we are paying millions of dollars for developing mines in foreign countries. The time has come when we ought to cease paying those bounties and let those industries look after themselves, which they are now well able to do.
- I wish particularly to make reference to the adverse balance of trade we have heard so much about. The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Poster) was not quite honest with the House and the country when he tried to blame the government because we bought so much more goods from the United States than we sold them. But if the policy of the government be wrong, it would be a very easy matter to rectify it by taking all these articles from the free list and putting them on the dutiable list. When the Fielding tariff was introduced in 1897, some 75 or 80 items were taken from the dutiable and put on the free list. If we put these back on the dutiable list, and charge them a heavy duty, we would stop a great deal of the importation from the United States which goes to swell the adverse balance of trade which my hon. friend spoke so much about. Well, I have taken the trouble to pick out the different items of the free list which we buy in the United States, and I invite the hon. member for North Toronto or any hon. member to make a motion to put any one of these items back on the dutiable list. Not one of them would dare to do so because, if he did, his supporters would not back him up; or if they did in this House, the supporters of the party in the country certainly would not. Almost every one of these items is required for the farmer, the fisherman or the manufacturer. They are nearly all for the benefit of the manufacturer and incidentally for the benefit of every consumer in the Dominion. The first item on the list is live animals. That is admited free for the improvement of the stock. Then there is the item of settlers' effects, would any one suggest putting them on the dutiable list? The next item is asphaltum, of which there is none in Canada. Would you suggest making every one who wants to use it pay a tax when it is not produced in Canada? Another item is books. What are those books? They are principally educational books, bibles, prayer books and books for the blind. Would any one suggest putting a tax on these ? Another item which amounts to nearly $4,000,000 is corn. That is used altogether by the farmers for feed and was made free for their special benefit. No one would suggest a heavy duty on the importation of corn for the feed of animals. Another item that runs up to
$15,000,000 is anthracite coal. That comes in free of duty. That comes into Canada from the United States free of duty. We do not mine anthracite coal in Canada to any extent, the only place I know of where it is mined being near Banff. There only a small amount is mined and it is shipped for only a short distance in that western country. Would any one suggest that we should prevent the importation of anthracite coal? There is scarcely a man in the House who does not use it, our people must have it, and placing a duty on it would noit stop the importation but simply cause the people of Canada to pay twice what they are now paying for it.
Is anthracite coal any cheaper in Canada since the duty was re- ' moved?

Yes, anthracite coal is cheaper in Canada by just the amount of the duty. If the duty was on it to-day it would be just that much dearer than it is. Another large item is cordage. That is used altogether for binding twine, for the farmers and fishermen. Cotton is another heavy- item running up to $7,000,000. .Would any one suggest that raw cotton be put on the dutiable list? No one would suggest such a thing. It is for the manufacturers and helping the manufacturer it incidentally helps every one, because there is no one who does not consume cotton to a certain extent. Drugs represent $5,000,000. Those are for the manufacturers altogether. Fertilizers, various articles for the fishermen, such as nets, flax, hemp and jute for the manufacture run into hundreds of thousands of dollars. Then we have green and ripe fruit coming into the country, $3,500,000. While there is fruit grown in Canada this comes in at a time when Canadian fruit is not ripe. In the western country we get carload after carload of that fruit, every little town brings in ripe and green fruits by the carload and to suggest putting on a duty would be absurd. Furs represent $2,000,000. Grasses, fibres and straws for manufactures represent $1,500,000. Rubber not produced in Canada, $2,500,000; hides, $1,500,000; iron, steel, &c., that is manufactured Swedish iron, wrought for horse shoe nails, represents nearly $5,000,000.
Will any hon. gentleman opposite suggest that these articles should be put on the dutiable list? If they cannot suggest that why should they complain all the time that the tariff of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance is not in the interest of this country and that we should not buy such an amount of goods from the United States when here on this list I have named of free goods there is over $85,000,000 and they go to make up practically what is called the adverse balance of trade. Not one hon member opposite would move that any o'

these items should be put on the dutiable list.
Oils come in free to the extent of about $2,000,000. Optical and mathematical instruments, paints and colours, plants and trees, resin, rennet, salt for the fishermen, seed bulbs all come in free and settlers' effects represent $5,761,000. This is not money that these settlers bring in but simply the goods they bring in. Would any one suggest that these items should be put on the dutiable list? I do not think so. We are spending money every year bringing in settlers. We are bringing in hundreds of thousands and naturally they bring in their effects. These go to swell the amount of goods we buy from the United States, but it does not show that the condition is not a good condition, that the tariff is not a good tariff and in the interest of the country. The very fact that gentlemen opposite would not move to change any one of these items, is, I think, proof conclusive that the items are in their proper place on the free list, and when we buy more goods from the United States than we sell to them it is because it pays us to do so and because we cannot get the goods as cheaply or as satisfactorily in any other place.
Raw silk for manufacturers, mill stones, turpentine, wood and manufactured wood come in free to the extent of $6,000,000. That affects us very much in the west. We import a great deal of lumber from the United States and all rough lumber comes in free of duty. No one in that part of the country would think of reimposing the duty on lumber simply because lumber is a necessity for the settlers and the cheaper we can get it into that part of the country the better. So I think the criticism levelled against the tariff is not a fair or reasonable criticism, and, as I said before, I do not believe that even the men who make the criticism think that it is right; it is made only and altogether for political purposes.
My hon. friends from Qu'Appelle (Mr. Lake) and Lisgar (Mr. W. H. Sharpe) dealt to a limited extent with the Hudson bay railway. Their criticism was that the road was not being built fast enough. I may say to my hon. friends that they need not worry at all, that road is going to be built. The Prime Minister has stated that the road was going to be built and I would ask my hon. friends to point to a single instance where the present Prime Minister has stated that the government were going to undertake and carry out a great public work, in which they have not done so. He never makes a promise that he does not carry out. The criticism has been that it is taking too long, that this promise was made in 1908. I am as anxious as any member in this House to see that railway built, and built as early as possible. I believe that Mr. TURRIFF.
railway will be a success, that the Hudson bay route will be a success, but it is not absolutely certain. I am free to admit that there is a certain amount of experiment about it, and if ever there was a case where a government was justified in taking every possible means, every measure it can,, to get full information about a route, to get the road built in the proper place, and' to have the terminals at the proper place, it is in connection with this Hudson bay road.
Have the government tried to find out anything in connection with this road?

Yes, I am pleased to be able to answer my hon. friend that the government have been hard at work for the last year and a half finding out the best possible route to Hudson bay, ascertaining the best place to end the road, whether at Fort Churchill or Fort York. It is a matter of great importance to this country to ascertain where the road should go. They have surveyed both routes, and during the past summer they were engaged in finding out whether the harbour at Fort York would be as good a harbour as that at Fort Churchill. If the harbour at Fort York is a good and satisfactory port it would be shorter and would save millions of dollars.
I do not think there is going to be any delay by taking the proper precautions in the first place. A great deal of money may be saved in this way-the spending of $100,000 in the making of proper surveys may be the means of saving millions upon millions. We do not want to be in the same position as the Canadian Pacific railway is in to-day-for that company is spending $10,000,000 every year to -change their route. Why, because, in the first place- and I am not throwing any blame on them now-the survey evidently was made hurriedly and not enough time, care or money was expended upon it. Had this mistake been avoided, millions of dollars would have been saved to-day. So, the government, I say, is amply justified in being careful to get full and absolute information. I do not believe for a moment that the right hon. Prime Minister or the government have any intention of delaying the building of that road. Why, even if the Hudson Bay route should not turn out to be as successful as we all hope it will, the road will pay for itself practically as a colonization road. I think we can all be proud of the fact that until you get away up into the polar regions there is no part of Canada in Which you can build a road but it will make a traffic for itself. We have that proven by the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway which extends from North Bay northward to connect with the Grand Trunk Pacific. The building of the Grand Trunk Pacific through Ontario and

Queibec will have this result that you will have a new Quebec and a new Ontario that, in 'the years to come, will rival the older settled portions of these provinces. The same thing applies to the Hudson Bay railway. You talk about sixteen millions of acres of clay land in the province of Ontario-and remember that sixteen million acres is a whole lot of land. Right on the line of the Hudson Bay road towards either Fort Churchill or Fort York, the road will go through a clay belt greater in extent than all the land in cultivation to-day in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta put together, which lands today are producing over 200,000,000 bushels of grain. There is a great extent of good land away north of Lake Winnipeg and on to Hudson bay. So, I say, the government is doing well in this matter, and hon. members opposite need not be a bit worried. That road is going to be built, and built as quickly as the government can find the proper place to build it. We shall soon know whether it is to be the great success we all hope it will be. I have no doubt about the matter, and I think that there can be very little doubt in the minds of any, of the ultimate success not only of the road but of the route. The road will afford us a much shorter route to the old country, it will afford us a better market and it will regulate freight rates. And so it will be a benefit not only to the west but to the eastern country as well. I am not going to take up more time. I congratulate the Minister of Finance (Air. Fielding) on his budget speech, but I think it is even more to the point to congratulate the country on having a Minister of Finance who is able to give such budget statements as the hon. gentleman has been giving us for the last thirteen years. And I say, long may he be spared to Canada to give just such satisfactory budget speeches as he delivered to the House the other day.
